stories.title: North Korean fake job interview led to $6.3B Binance heist
stories.reason: Record $6.3B crypto theft; attackers used an internal AI tool to pivot between compromised engineer machines, a concrete AI-enabled lateral-movement detail that lands squarely on the AI x cyber line. Several other pool entries cover the same story — picked for best primary-source detail.
key_facts: $6.3B stolen from Binance, the largest crypto theft on record

Attack began in June 2026 with a malicious Homebrew supply-chain download; escalated via a September fake-job-interview social-engineering campaign (fake HR rep, fake CEO) delivering malware disguised as a coding 'assignment'
Malware swapped a legit pyenv component, opened a C2 connection, evaded endpoint tools
Oct 20: attackers used the compromised machine plus an internal AI tool to pivot to two more engineers' machines
Oct 29: a stolen container deployment token was used to deploy a container that ran the theft script
FBI attributes the operation to TraderTraitor/Lazarus Group (North Korea)

stories.title: AI is forcing us to pay off 40 years of technical debt
stories.reason: 1046-point HN thread on AI collapsing the cost of exploiting decades-old bugs, anchored in a real, named vulnerability (PHP2Shell) hitting NASA/Wikipedia/White House — concrete AI-assisted exploit-dev story, not a rumor.
key_facts: PHP2Shell: a PHP out-of-memory bug reported in 2024, long considered merely crash-prone, was turned into full remote code execution in late Oct 2026, affecting NASA, Wikipedia, White House, WordPress and Drupal sites
Security firm Calif (an OpenAI-sponsored PHP audit) weaponized it in two weeks with AI assistance; a patch shipped before exploitation, but took 4 engineers 2 months to build
Columbia's Suman Jana: AI is especially good at the tedious memory-mapping reasoning the exploit required
Anthropic (Oct 22) published an LLM-writes-patch plus non-LLM-proof-checker formal-verification approach as a proposed remedy
Johns Hopkins' Matthew Green predicts a much worse incident, possibly around early 2027, before funding/action follows

stories.title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines
stories.reason: Primary-source (Project Zero) head-to-head data on AI vs classic fuzzing for real browser-engine bugs — a rare quantified comparison, not a vendor pitch.
key_facts: Google Project Zero compared Fuzzilli (traditional generative fuzzer) vs BigSleep (LLM-based) on V8 production bugs, April-Sept 2026
Actionable vulnerabilities: Fuzzilli 37, BigSleep 45; only ~25% overlap (20 of 81 actionable bugs found by both)
In a controlled rediscovery test, BigSleep found ~62% of 112 historic Fuzzilli bugs (70% with prompt variants); no sign of memorizing pre-2026 bugs
BigSleep runs once daily with a 1-2 day reporting lag; Fuzzilli runs continuously, catching changes within hours
Conclusion: the two approaches are complementary, and agentic systems' share of discoveries is expected to grow

stories.title: Hiding Capabilities in AI Models
stories.reason: Concrete, code-backed research showing provable limits on eliciting backdoored capabilities from model weights — a direct hit on model-supply-chain-compromise, the always-surface AI x cyber sub-topic, not a bare arxiv listing since a PyTorch POC and models were released.
key_facts: Paper 'AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities' (arXiv 2610.13928) shows capabilities can be embedded as encrypted neural networks inside host model weights, decrypted only by a secret trigger, using cryptographic 'digital lockers'
Resisted elicitation via fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training in PyTorch proof-of-concept tests on a chemical-reaction-prediction proxy task
Authors released their models to support defense research; undermines the core assumption behind pre-deployment capability audits

stories.title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
stories.reason: Primary-source Anthropic research with a real open-source release addressing a concrete inference-serving trust problem (verifying you got the model you paid for) — directly on the 'how models are served' interest, with hard numbers.
key_facts: Anthropic's FlashProve: open-source (Apache 2.0) zkSNARK-based 'provable inference' prototype, letting a low-compute user verify a response came from specific committed model weights without learning them
On Llama 4 Maverick (400B MoE, 4-bit): ~110 tok/s proving throughput on one H100, ~18.8MB proof per 1024-token window, 70-95x GPU overhead vs vLLM
One-time offline commitment setup: ~39 min, covers ~16M requests; verification ~17s on 24 CPU threads
Prior open-source baseline (VerInf) took 14.3 hours for 1000 tokens with a 93.6GB proof — FlashProve is dramatically faster/smaller
Limitations: covers only integer weights under greedy decoding, 1024-token context cap, side-channels out of scope

stories.title: Nvidia RTX Spark encrypted firmware slows inference speed to 35% on Linux
stories.reason: Concrete, benchmarked inference-serving regression on real hardware (65-79% throughput loss) caused by vendor firmware DRM — directly on the 'how models are served' interest with hard measured numbers.
key_facts: MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI Plus: Nvidia's Windows-only 'Platform Controllers and Framework' encrypts the GPU power table, so Linux can't read it and caps GPU clocks when plugged in
Plugged-in clock: ~780MHz on Linux vs ~2.2GHz on Windows (-65%); GPT-OSS-120B throughput 13.9 vs 65.4 tok/s (-79%); vLLM 8-client throughput 39.5 vs 127 tok/s (-69%)
On battery, Linux reaches ~61-67 tok/s, close to Windows — the regression is specific to AC power plus the encrypted firmware table
No real Linux-native fix exists yet; one community attempt at the power table caused a kernel panic

stories.title: Ripple-65B Preview: U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding
stories.reason: A small open-weight model beating much larger ones on agentic coding at a fraction of the training cost — an efficiency-of-serving story with real comparative benchmark numbers.
key_facts: Ripple-65B Preview (Ricursive Intelligence): dense 65B-param transformer, 12T pretraining tokens, 1M context, open-weight

Scores 80.52 on TerminalBench 2.1, narrowly ahead of Reflection Beam (501B, 80.1) and well ahead of Meta Muse Spark Open (816B, 76.4) and Nvidia Nemotron 3 Ultra (550B, 56.4) despite being far smaller
Company claims $32M total R&D cost (~1/10th of prior open-weight SOTA) using ~1.4M RL rollouts, ~70x fewer than Reflection Beam's reported spend

stories.title: Letting users trust their own MCP clients, without opening a phishing hole
stories.reason: Concrete, running fix for a real, exploited MCP OAuth phishing pattern (114/119 servers vulnerable, a real Square account takeover) — exactly the agent/MCP-attack-chain-with-PoC always-surface topic, from the defensive side.
key_facts: A May 2026 study found 114 of 119 OAuth-enabled MCP servers accept arbitrary redirect_uri values from any anonymous client registration — PKCE doesn't block it since the attacker initiates the flow
Real incident cited: an account takeover against Square's MCP server (reported Jan 2026) via this pattern

Proposed/shipped fix (live on Stream Vessel's MCP page): self-registration stays open, but each signed-in user adds up to 10 exact HTTPS redirect URIs to their own trust list; unknown redirects get a typed-host confirmation page instead of a silent redirect
MCP's 2026-07-28 draft spec deprecates Dynamic Client Registration for Client ID Metadata Documents, which the post argues still doesn't solve per-user intent
